 TO THE HONORABLE ADMINISTRATIVE LAW JUDGES:

       Intervenors Solana Ranch Company, Solana Development, LP, Don Al Ringler, and

CEDON Realty, Ltd. (collectively, the “Solana Intervenors” or “Solana”) (Party No. 217),

respectfully submit this Initial Brief in support of Route 392 and would show the following:

I.     INTRODUCTION AND STATEMENT OF THE CASE

       Oncor Electric Delivery Company LLC and LCRA Transmission Service Corporation

(collectively, “Applicants”) filed a joint application to amend their Certificates of Convenience

and Necessity for the Bell County East Switch to Big Hill Substation 765-kV Transmission Line

Project spanning fifteen counties. This Initial Brief will focus on issues relating to the Route

(Preliminary Order No. 8) that best meets the regulatory and statutory criteria. Solana

acknowledges there are legitimate concerns that have been raised by several parties relating to the

need for Import Path 2. Solana did not submit direct evidence on these issues, and so does not

attempt to evaluate the evidence relating to them here. Solana reserves the right to reply to

arguments on the need issues (Preliminary Order Issues 5, 6, and 7) in its Reply Brief. Applicants

have identified Route 894 as the route that best meets the applicable statutory and regulatory

criteria. The evidence adduced throughout this proceeding and admitted at the Hearing on the

Merits demonstrates that Route 894 fails to satisfy the statutory and regulatory criteria governing

route selection. The Commission should select Route 392 instead.

       Solana Development, LP is the owner and developer of Solana Ranch, a large-scale master-

planned community located in Williamson and Bell Counties along the Interstate 35 corridor

between Georgetown and Temple. The property encompasses approximately 8,000 acres, most of

which is dedicated to an active development effort planned to include approximately 14,000

residential units together with commercial, civic, recreational, and open space uses. Solana Ranch

Co. owns land adjacent to that owned by Solana Development, LP. The land owned by Solana

PUC DOCKET NO. 59475; SOAH DOCKET 473-26-16349; INITIAL BRIEF OF THE SOLANA INTERVENORS
PAGE 1 OF 18
 Ranch Co. will be preserved in its legacy agricultural and natural uses as described in the testimony

of Michael Michaux. The existing extensive wildlife habitat on the Solana Ranch Co. property

will be integrated with designated wildlife habitat on the Solana Development, LP property.

Among the other negative impacts of Route 894, the integrated wildlife habitat would be adversely

affected by the bisection of the properties. Don Al Ringler and CEDON Realty, Ltd. own Ringler

Ranch, a separate adjacent property in Bell County managed for wildlife, conservation, and family

use, that would be directly and adversely affected by the introduction of HVTL infrastructure in

the same area.

       Route 894 bisects the developable core of the Solana Development property and the

reserved Solana Ranch. It also places major 765-kV transmission infrastructure immediately

adjacent to Ringler Ranch. The Solana Intervenors oppose Route 894 and any route utilizing Links

E52, F1, F20, F21, F32, or F33. Route 894 fails to satisfy the statutory routing criteria set forth in

PURA § 37.056(c)(4)(A)-(D) and PUC Substantive Rule 25.101(b)(3)(B). The record establishes

that Route 392 best meets those criteria, and the Solana Intervenors request that the Commission

grant a certificate of convenience and necessity for Route 392.

II.    THE COMMISSION SHOULD ORDER A ROUTE UTILIZING A NORTHERN
       COLORADO RIVER CROSSING.

       The proposed transmission line must cross the Colorado River at some location. That much

is not in dispute. The threshold policy-level question the ALJs and Commission must answer is

where that crossing should occur. As Andrew H. Sansom, Ph.D., who served for twelve years as

Executive Director of the Texas Parks and Wildlife Department and brings decades of professional

experience in conservation, water resources, and public land stewardship in Texas, testified: “From




PUC DOCKET NO. 59475; SOAH DOCKET 473-26-16349; INITIAL BRIEF OF THE SOLANA INTERVENORS
PAGE 2 OF 18
 a conservation perspective, the primary question is where that crossing can occur in a manner that

does the least harm to the character of the river and to the surrounding environment.” 1

           The Colorado River in the central portion of the Study Area flows through the Hill Country

and its associated landscapes, where it is characterized by rugged terrain, scenic vistas, and

relatively intact riparian environments. The river and its corridors support a diversity of plant and

animal life and provide important ecological, recreational, and aesthetic values to the State of

Texas as a whole. The Colorado is the longest river in Texas. It provides water to one of the nation’s

most populous metropolitan areas, powers cities, and creates recreational areas of cultural

significance, including our newest state park. Indeed, this reach of the river is home to Colorado

Bend State Park, one of the most treasured State Parks in the State. 2 It also hosts the state parks

system’s newest jewel, Post Oak Ridge State Park. Both these parks are surrounded by potential

links in this Study Area.

           The routing materials identify six locations within the study area at which the alternative

routes would cross the Colorado River.

           Of the six crossing locations identified in the Study Area, only one satisfies those

principles: Link U3, the northernmost crossing, which parallels an existing electric transmission

 line rather than introducing an entirely above ground disturbance across the Colorado River. 7

Every other crossing location would establish a new point of disturbance in a previously unaffected

reach of the river. 8

        The five remaining crossings—Links U2, J11, J26, J22, and J31—share the undesirable

characteristic that they would introduce new transmission infrastructure into undeveloped portions

of the Colorado River environment, several of them in close proximity to Colorado Bend State

Park, Post Oak Ridge State Park, and other highly valued scenic and recreational resources. 9 The

record establishes that Links J11, J26, and J22 present particular concerns by virtue of their

proximity to the parks, and that Link J22—the Colorado River crossing utilized by Route 894—

presents additional viewshed impacts on the newly established Post Oak Ridge State Park that

were developed in detail at the hearing. 10 The Commission should reject any route that utilizes

Links J11, J22, or J26 as its Colorado River crossing, 11 and give serious scrutiny to any route

utilizing U2 or J31.

III.    DR. RHODES’S TESTIMONY DEMONSTRATES THAT ROUTE 392 BEST
        MEETS THE STATUTORY AND REGULATORY CRITERIA.

        A. The U3 and Pipeline Avoidance Criteria Eliminate Route 894 and Narrow the
           Field to Four Viable Candidates.

        Dr. Joshua Rhodes, Ph.D., testified on behalf of the Solana Intervenors regarding route

evaluation criteria, the crossing of the Colorado River, and the comparative performance of the

filed routes. Dr. Rhodes also identified the Colorado River crossing as the most consequential

geographic constraint in the study area. River crossings limit routing flexibility and carry outsized

environmental and visual consequences. Link U3 crosses the Colorado River in a location that

 parallels existing electric transmission infrastructure. Every other available Colorado River

crossing link would establish a new corridor where none currently exists. Dr. Rhodes testified that

applying Link U3 as the preferred Colorado River crossing is consistent with the Commission’s

routing principles favoring utilization of compatible rights-of-way and minimization of

incremental impacts when alternative options remain available. Applying that criterion precludes

the use of Route 894. 12

         From the remaining routes, Dr. Rhodes applied a second screening criterion: pipeline

paralleling. Dr. Rhodes testified that pipeline paralleling is no longer a preferred routing

characteristic because of the cathodic protection required to mitigate stray voltage, and that

prudence counsels particular caution given that the proposed line will operate at a higher voltage

than any existing transmission line in the state. Routes 391, 408, 420, 589, and 592 each include

extended segments of pipeline paralleling and are therefore less favorable. 13 Dr. Rhodes further

declined to rely on the Applicants’ apparent property boundary paralleling dataset, finding it to be

of limited validity as a differentiating metric. After excluding property line paralleling from

consideration, Routes 389, 399, and 588 performed materially less favorably than the remaining

candidates due to approximately ten fewer miles of paralleling with compatible infrastructure such

as roads and transmission corridors. The field thus narrowed to four routes warranting further

comparison: Routes 392, 402, 410, and 416. 14

         B. Route 392 Outperforms Routes 402, 410, and 416 on Cost, Habitable Structures,
            and Environmental Criteria

         Among the four remaining candidates, Routes 410 and 416 are estimated to cost

approximately $22 to $23 million more than Routes 392 and 402, and are approximately 4.5 miles

more open water features, and a greater number of recorded cultural resource sites. Known rare or

unique plant locations fall within the rights-of-way of Routes 410 and 416, while Routes 392 and

402 have none. Routes 410 and 416 also carry a greater interaction with aviation-related facilities.

Solana Ex. 4 at 17. Routes 392 and 402 maintain comparable levels of compatible infrastructure

paralleling relative to Routes 410 and 416 despite their shorter length, confirming that the cost and

environmental advantages of Routes 392 and 402 do not come at the expense of corridor

efficiency. 15

        Between Routes 392 and 402, Route 392 performs better on habitable structures based on

the Applicants’ data. Dr. Rhodes acknowledged concerns about the accuracy and consistency of

that dataset but treated it as directionally informative for purposes of the comparison. 16 Route 392

also keeps the line to the northern extent of the San Saba River watershed, reducing the degree to

which the transmission line traverses the core of that river valley—a consideration directly relevant

to the Commission’s evaluation of environmental integrity, community values, and aesthetics

under PURA § 37.056(c)(4)(A) and (C). On redirect, Dr. Rhodes further confirmed that when

Route 392 is compared against Route 894 on total compatible infrastructure paralleling, Route 392

performs better. 17

        C. No Cross-Examination Blunted Dr. Rhodes’s Opinion.

        Multiple parties cross-examined Dr. Rhodes, focusing primarily on two challenges: (1) that

his use of Link U3 as a threshold screening criterion reflected a “personal preference” rather than

a principled analytical judgment, and (2) that Route 392 carries more habitable structures than

Route 894. Neither challenge undermines his conclusions. On the first point, Dr. Rhodes confirmed

 on redirect that his recommendation reflected professional judgment, not personal preference, and

that Link U3 is the best Colorado River crossing because existing transmission infrastructure is

already located there. 18 In any event, the recommendation for a northern Colorado River crossing

utilizing existing transmission infrastructure is not a position unique to Dr. Rhodes. Commission

Staff witness John Poole and Brady Creek Intervenors’ witness Dr. Andrew Sansom both

independently reached the same conclusion: Link U3 is the superior Colorado River crossing

because it parallels existing HVTL transmission infrastructure rather than establishing a new

corridor.

         On the habitable structures differential, Dr. Rhodes was questioned on the reported count

of 138 habitable structures within 500 feet of Route 392 against 85 for Route 894. Dr. Rhodes

responded that he identified errors on both sides of the ledger—structures counted that were not

present, and structures not counted that were—and that the Applicants’ underlying dataset lacks

the consistency required to bear the weight Applicants place on it. 19 That position is consistent

with the broader evidentiary record, which establishes that the Applicants’ habitable structure data

contains material discrepancies. The cross-examination on this point confirmed the concern about

the reliability of Applicants’ data rather than resolving any issue in favor of Route 894.

IV.      ROUTE 894 IS INCOMPATIBLE WITH THE SOLANA RANCH COMMUNITY
         AND THE STATUTORY FACTORS SET FORTH IN PURA § 37.056(c)(4)(A)–(D).

         A. Solana Ranch: History, Stewardship, and the Development Plan.

         Solana Ranch is an approximately 8,000-acre property located in Williamson and Bell

Counties along the Interstate 35 corridor between Georgetown and Temple. Frank and Retta

Michaux founded the Ranch in 1950, and it has remained under continuous family ownership

 across four generations. Mike Michaux testified that the Michaux family has operated a cattle

operation on the Ranch continuously for 76 years, and that stewardship of the land has been central

to the family’s management approach from the beginning. 20 That stewardship record is

documented by a series of conservation awards spanning more than five decades, including the

Lone Star Land Steward Award from Texas Parks and Wildlife in 2017. The Ranch contains

significant natural features—Salado Creek, Rumsey Creek, Buttermilk Creek, 100-foot limestone

bluffs, and mature legacy tree cover—as well as a 256-acre conservation easement protecting the

Salado salamander. 21

         In 2021, the Michaux family partnered with DMB Development LLC, a nationally

recognized developer of large-scale master-planned communities, to begin planning a

development that would respond to the region’s rapid growth while preserving the Ranch's most

significant natural and historic features. Mary Alexander, Principal and Executive Vice President

of DMB Development, testified that the development plan was designed around the Ranch's rolling

topography, natural drainage features, and environmentally sensitive areas, with those features

incorporated as organizing elements of the community rather than obstacles to be cleared. 22 The

resulting plan encompasses up to 7,000 developable acres and calls for approximately 14,000

residential units together with commercial, civic, open space, and recreational uses. 23

         B. Solana Ranch Is an Active Master-Planned Community.

many stakeholders having poured thousands of working hours and millions of dollars over nearly

six years, with substantial governmental approvals, executed infrastructure agreements, and

          C. Route 894 Bisects the Developable Core of the Ranch, Conflicting with All
            Applicable Routing Criteria.

         Route 894 runs directly through the interior of Solana Ranch, bisecting the most

developable areas of the property through Links E52, F1, F20, F31, F32, F33, and related

segments. Alexander testified that Route 894 does not follow any boundary line, existing

infrastructure right-of-way, or discernible natural land contour, and cuts directly through areas

designated for a community Town Center commercial core, residential uses, and open space. 30

         That poor alignment directly implicates factors (A) and (B) of PURA § 37.056(c)(4), which

requires route selection to moderate the impact of the line on the affected community, taking into

account community values and aesthetic values. A 765-kV transmission line bisecting the

geographic and functional center of a 14,000-unit planned community is categorically inconsistent

with that standard. Route selection also requires minimizing the impact of line on the use and

development of land, including avoidance of bisecting property where possible. Route 894 does

the opposite: it cuts through the interior of the Ranch in a manner that, as Alexander testified,

would destroy the cohesion and functionality of the community as designed, force redesign of

roads and infrastructure, reduce total developable area, and delay or jeopardize the project’s overall

feasibility. 31

         Route 894 also conflicts with the Commission’s imperative to avoid or minimize adverse

effects on the natural environment, including scenic areas and water resources. Route 894 crosses

Buttermilk, Rumsey, and Salado Creeks, which flow above the Edwards Aquifer recharge zone,

and would affect areas the development plan was specifically designed to protect. 32 The cost

consequences of Route 894 to Solana Ranch and to the Counties that have committed to support

V.         THE CHARACTER AND CONDITION OF THE AFFECTED LANDSCAPE
           CONFIRM THAT ROUTE 894 IS THE WRONG CHOICE.

           A.       Photographs of the Solana Ranch.

           The photographs admitted as part of Mike Michaux’s testimony provide the Commission

with direct visual context for what Route 894 would affect. The aerial photograph below captures

Rumsey Creek flowing into Salado Creek across the open pasture and wooded terrain of Solana

Ranch—the same creek system that runs through the 256-acre conservation easement established

to protect the Salado salamander. The sunset photograph depicts the ridgeline along Main Road

that Link F1 of Route 894 would traverse. Other photos show Rumsey Creek at the conservation

easement area, with the limestone bluffs, mature tree cover, and spring-fed water features that

Michaux testified make this property both environmentally significant and visually irreplaceable.

           These photographs only begin to illustrate why Route 894’s proposed bisection of this

undisturbed landscape conflicts with the Commission’s obligation under PURA § 37.056(c)(4)(A)

and (C) to account for aesthetic values, scenic areas, and the integrity of natural resources.

          B.       Ringler Ranch: Applicants’ Desktop Analysis Fails to Account for the
                  Community and Environmental Character of this Part of Bell County.

         Don Al Ringler testified that his approximately 270-acre property in Bell County near

Salado contains rolling terrain, wooded areas, restored native grasslands, two converging creek

corridors, limestone bluffs, and elevated scenic views of the surrounding countryside. 38 Since

2012, Ringler has actively managed the property for wildlife habitat through participation in Texas

Parks and Wildlife programs, including Managed Lands Deer Permits and Pastures for Upland

Birds, and has invested substantial resources in invasive cedar removal, native prairie restoration,

and water source improvement. 39 Route 894 does not directly cross Ringler Ranch, but Link F20

places major 765-kV transmission infrastructure immediately adjacent to the property, and Link

F21, which the Solana Intervenors also oppose, would bisect it directly. Ringler testified that the

proposed alignments in this area do not follow existing infrastructure corridors, property

boundaries, or natural dividing features, and that introducing transmission infrastructure of this

scale would permanently alter the scenic character and ecological integrity of this portion of Bell

County.40 The Ringler Ranch record reinforces the same statutory values at issue for Solana Ranch:

this is a part of Bell County that landowners have spent years improving, preserving, and

protecting, and the routing analysis conducted by Applicants did not meaningfully account for it.

Applicants conducted a desktop analysis that missed all of it, and the record reflects no meaningful

effort to understand what was actually on the ground before Route 894 was selected. Any

recommendation that Route 894 “best-meets” the statutory and regulatory requirements for route

selection fails to understand these important issues.

 VI.    CONCLUSION

       Route 894 fails to satisfy the requirements of PURA § 37.056(c)(4)(A)–(D) and PUC

Substantive Rule 25.101(b)(3)(B). Applicants selected Route 894 based primarily on cost and

habitable structure counts — two metrics that the evidence in this proceeding has placed in serious

question. That selection ignored the Colorado River crossing principle supported by Commission

Staff and multiple intervenor witnesses, disregarded the unreliability of the underlying data on

which Applicants’ comparative analysis is predicated, and failed to account for the active master-

planned community, the conservation history, and the irreplaceable natural and scenic resources

that Route 894 would bisect and permanently damage.

       Route 392 is the superior route. It utilizes Link U3 at the Colorado River, avoiding the

creation of a new crossing corridor where none currently exists. It avoids extended pipeline

paralleling. It performs favorably on cost, habitable structures, and environmental criteria relative

to every remaining candidate in Dr. Rhodes’ analysis. It does not traverse the developable core of

Solana Ranch, does not place major transmission infrastructure adjacent to Ringler Ranch and

undeveloped stretches of undisturbed private property, and does not threaten the conservation

values and community character that the statutory routing criteria were designed to protect. The

ALJs should recommend Route 392.

the foregoing and issue a Proposal for Decision recommending Route 392.

I.     INTRODUCTION AND STATEMENT OF THE CASE

       Oncor Electric Delivery Company LLC and LCRA Transmission Service Corporation

(collectively, "Applicants") filed a joint application to amend their Certificates of Convenience

and Necessity for the Bell County East Switch to Big Hill Substation 765-kV Transmission Line

Project spanning fifteen counties. This Initial Brief will focus on issues relating to the Route

(Preliminary Order No. 8) that best meets the regulatory and statutory criteria. Solana

acknowledges there are legitimate concerns that have been raised by several parties relating to the

need for Import Path 2. Solana did not submit direct evidence on these issues, and so does not

attempt to evaluate the evidence relating to them here. Solana reserves the right to reply to

arguments on the need issues (Preliminary Order Issues 5,6, and 7) in its Reply Brief. Applicants

have identified Route 894 as the route that best meets the applicable statutory and regulatory

criteria. The evidence adduced throughout this proceeding and admitted at the Hearing on the

Merits demonstrates that Route 894 fails to satisfy the statutory and regulatory criteria governing

route selection. The Commission should select Route 392 instead.

       Solana Development, LP is the owner and developer of Solana Ranch, a large-scale master-

planned community located in Williamson and Bell Counties along the Interstate 35 corridor

between Georgetown and Temple. The property encompasses approximately 8,000 acres, most of

which is dedicated to an active development effort planned to include approximately 14,000

residential units together with commercial, civic, recreational, and open space uses. Solana Ranch

Co. owns land adj acent to that owned by Solana Development, LP. The land owned by Solana

II.    THE COMMISSION SHOULD ORDER A ROUTE UTILIZING A NORTHERN
       COLORADO RIVER CROSSING.

       The proposed transmission line must cross the Colorado River at some location. That much

is not in dispute. The threshold policy-level question the ALJs and Commission must answer is

where that crossing should occur. As Andrew H. Sansom, Ph.D., who served for twelve years as

Executive Director ofthe Texas Parks and Wildlife Department and brings decades of professional

experience in conservation, water resources, and public land stewardship in Texas, testified: "From

        The Colorado River in the central portion ofthe Study Area flows through the Hill Country

and its associated landscapes, where it is characterized by rugged terrain, scenic vistas, and

relatively intact riparian environments. The river and its corridors support a diversity of plant and

animal life and provide important ecological, recreational, and aesthetic values to the State of

Texas as a whole. The Colorado is the longest river in Texas. It provides water to one of the nation's

most populous metropolitan areas, powers cities, and creates recreational areas of cultural

significance, including our newest state park. Indeed, this reach of the river is home to Colorado

Bend State Park, one of the most treasured State Parks in the State. 2 It also hosts the state parks

system's newest jewel, Post Oak Ridge State Park. Both these parks are surrounded by potential

links in this Study Area.

 VI.    CONCLUSION

       Route 894 fails to satisfy the requirements of PURA § 37.056(c)(4)(A)-(D) and PUC

Substantive Rule 25.101(b)(3)(B). Applicants selected Route 894 based primarily on cost and

habitable structure counts - two metrics that the evidence in this proceeding has placed in serious

question. That selection ignored the Colorado River crossing principle supported by Commission

Staff and multiple intervenor witnesses, disregarded the unreliability of the underlying data on

which Applicants' comparative analysis is predicated, and failed to account for the active master-

planned community, the conservation history, and the irreplaceable natural and scenic resources

that Route 894 would bisect and permanently damage.

       Route 392 is the superior route. It utilizes Link U3 at the Colorado River, avoiding the

creation of a new crossing corridor where none currently exists. It avoids extended pipeline

paralleling. It performs favorably on cost, habitable structures, and environmental criteria relative

to every remaining candidate in Dr. Rhodes' analysis. It does not traverse the developable core of

Solana Ranch, does not place major transmission infrastructure adjacent to Ringler Ranch and

undeveloped stretches of undisturbed private property, and does not threaten the conservation

values and community character that the statutory routing criteria were designed to protect. The

ALJs should recommend Route 392.
